sections.body_md:
The Hessian is the derivative of the gradient. Multiplying it by a direction \(d\) is therefore the directional derivative of the gradient map. Automatic differentiation can take that derivative without writing the matrix down.

The usual arrangement is forward-over-reverse. A reverse sweep builds the gradient, with its own computational graph. A forward sweep then pushes the seed \(d\) through that graph. The tangent of the gradient is \(H_f(x)\, d\). Reverse-over-forward does the same job when the direction is held constant: forward mode builds the scalar \(\nabla f(x)^{T} d\), and a reverse sweep differentiates that scalar with respect to \(x\).

Either product costs about as much as one gradient. The full matrix is \(n\) such products, one per column. A method that only needs curvature in particular directions never forms those columns.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
If \(g(x) = \nabla f(x)\), then \(g'(x)\, d = H_f(x)\, d\). Forward-over-reverse evaluates that directional derivative. With \(d\) independent of \(x\),
\[
\nabla_x \bigl(\nabla f(x)^{T} d\bigr) = H_f(x)\, d
\]
as well, which is reverse-over-forward. The quadratic form \(d^{T} H_f(x)\, d\) is the second directional derivative of \(f\), obtained from one product and one inner product. The \(i\)th column of the Hessian is the product with the \(i\)th coordinate vector.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Take \(f(x, y) = 3x^2 + xy\). The Hessian is constant, with first row \((6, 1)\) and second row \((1, 0)\). For the direction \((2, -1)\) the product entries 11 and 2 are \(6\cdot 2 + 1\cdot(-1) = 11\) and \(1\cdot 2 + 0\cdot(-1) = 2\). The quadratic form on this direction is \(2\cdot 11 + (-1)\cdot 2 = 20\). A forward difference of the gradient in this direction, divided by a small step, approaches \((11, 2)\) and does not produce the other column. One direction yields one vector.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: The product \(H d\) is not the gradient and not the first directional derivative \(\nabla f^{T} d\). Those are first-order. Reading the first column as the diagonal of the matrix swaps the off-diagonal entry with a diagonal entry that the direction did not select. One product does not fill the matrix. Forming every entry by finite differences costs many more function evaluations than \(n\) gradient-like products, and it adds truncation. If the direction depends on \(x\) and you differentiate it as well, reverse-over-forward picks up extra terms that are not \(H d\).

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Newton's method solves \(H_f(x)\, d = -\nabla f(x)\). An iterative solver for that system needs only products with \(H_f(x)\). Conjugate gradients are built for exactly that interface. The second-order optimality test, by contrast, wants to know whether the Hessian is positive semidefinite. Products can probe that question along chosen directions, while the full matrix remains the direct certificate.
